stem: An engineer sets spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges on a LoadBalancer service and expects the same CIDR restriction to apply to the NodePort and ClusterIP services created alongside it. With default Cilium behaviour, what actually happens?

The CIDRs apply to all three service types automatically.
The CIDRs are rejected unless bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is set to true.

explanation: By default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges only apply to the LoadBalancer service, not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP service installed along with it.

optionRationale.b: The default does not extend to NodePort either; only the LoadBalancer service is covered.
optionRationale.c: Applying the CIDRs to all externally exposed types requires opting in, for example via bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the field is rejected; it describes a default scoping behaviour and two ways to change it.

stem: A team wants the CIDR list in loadBalancerSourceRanges to block traffic from certain CIDRs while allowing everything else. Which annotation and value achieve this?

options.text: service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy: deny

service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer
bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true

explanation: Cilium supports turning the list into a deny-list through the service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy annotation, which accepts allow or deny; setting it to deny blocks traffic from the listed CIDRs while allowing the rest.

optionRationale.b: The allow value is the default behaviour, which treats the list as an allow-list rather than a deny-list.
optionRationale.c: The service.cilium.io/type annotation is used to avoid creating corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not to invert the CIDR policy.
optionRationale.d: bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes is a Helm option that propagates the CIDRs to all externally exposed service types; it does not turn the list into a deny-list.

stem: A platform team has a global service in cluster 1 with `service.cilium.io/affinity` set to `local`. All local backends in cluster 1 are healthy. A client in cluster 1 curls the global service. What does it observe?

options.text: Replies come only from pods in cluster 1, because the local endpoints are preferred while they remain available and healthy.
Replies come from pods in both clusters, because the affinity annotation only affects endpoints in the remote cluster.
Replies come only from pods in cluster 2, because `local` means the local cluster is excluded from load-balancing.
Replies alternate strictly between cluster 1 and cluster 2, because `local` enables round-robin across clusters.

explanation: With the annotation value `local`, the Global Service load-balances across healthy local backends and only uses remote endpoints if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy. The excerpt's step 2 confirms that from cluster 1 you will see replies from pods in cluster 1 only.

optionRationale.b: The annotation does affect which endpoints are preferred; the excerpt shows cluster 1 clients getting replies from cluster 1 only, not from both clusters.
optionRationale.c: `local` prefers endpoints from the local cluster, not the remote one; `remote` is the value that prefers remote endpoints.

The HTTPRoute configuration was correct and accepted.
All referenced secrets were found and have permission for use.
The route has been programmed into Envoy by the Cilium Gateway controller.

explanation: For HTTPRoute status, the excerpt lists `ResolvedRefs` as meaning the referenced services were found and are valid references. `Accepted` is the condition covering whether the HTTPRoute configuration was correct and accepted.

optionRationale.b: That is the meaning of the `Accepted` condition type for an HTTPRoute, not `ResolvedRefs`.
optionRationale.c: That description belongs to `ResolvedRefs` on the Gateway's status conditions, which concerns referenced secrets, not the HTTPRoute's service references.
optionRationale.d: Programming into Envoy is described by the `Programmed` condition on the Gateway, not by `ResolvedRefs` on an HTTPRoute.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: ``ResolvedRefs``: The referenced services were found and are valid references.

stem: A Gateway's status shows a condition with Status set to false, and you want to understand why. Which fields does the excerpt say give more information?

options.text: The `Message` and `Reason` fields.
The `Type` and `Status` fields.
The `Controller Name` and `Parent Ref` fields.
The `Attached Routes` count on the listener.

explanation: The excerpt states that if any of the conditions are set to false, the `Message` and `Reason` fields give more information. `Type` identifies the condition type and `Status` is the boolean, so neither explains the failure.

optionRationale.b: `Type` indicates the condition type and `Status` indicates with a boolean whether the condition type is met; they do not carry the explanatory detail.
optionRationale.c: `Controller Name` and `Parent Ref` identify the controller and the parent gateway reference, not the reason for a false condition.
optionRationale.d: `Attached Routes` shows the number of routes successfully attached to the listener, not why a condition is false.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If any of these conditions are set to false, the ``Message`` and ``Reason`` fields give more information.

stem: An engineer is running a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available, and wants the Cilium ingress controller's Envoy listener reachable directly on the host network. After enabling host network mode via Helm, which statement describes the resulting Service configuration?

options.text: The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode is automatically disabled, because the two modes are mutually exclusive.
A LoadBalancer Service is still created, but it is bound only to the loopback interface.
A NodePort Service is retained alongside the host listener so that both paths remain available.
The Service type is switched to ExternalName so that the host listener can be reached by DNS name.

explanation: Host network mode and the LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode cannot coexist: enabling host network mode automatically disables the Service-based mode. The listener is then exposed on all interfaces rather than on a Service.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 and/or ::), not restricted to loopback, and says nothing about retaining a LoadBalancer Service.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the two modes are mutually exclusive, so a NodePort Service is not retained alongside the host listener.
optionRationale.d: No ExternalName Service type is mentioned anywhere in the excerpt; the Service mode is disabled, not converted.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium ingress controller host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

stem: An engineer enables host network mode and wants the shared HTTP listener to be reachable on a host port different from the shared listener port, while leaving the other shared listeners on the default. Which Helm value should be set?

options.text: ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort
ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort
ingressController.hostNetwork.tlsPassthroughPort
ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port

explanation: The httpPort value sets the host network port for the shared HTTP listener specifically. If it is unset or 0, the sharedListenerPort value is used instead, which is why the other listeners stay on the default.

optionRationale.a: sharedListenerPort sets the port for the Envoy listener generally and is the fallback for the individual listeners; changing it would move all shared listeners, not just HTTP.
optionRationale.c: tlsPassthroughPort applies to the shared TLS passthrough listener, not the HTTP listener.
optionRationale.d: This is an annotation applied per Ingress resource for dedicated ingress, not a Helm value for the shared HTTP listener.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: ``ingressController.hostNetwork.httpPort``: Host network port to expose the shared HTTP listener. If unset or ``0``, ``sharedListenerPort`` is used.

stem: A cluster runs the Cilium ingress controller in dedicated mode, and several Ingress resources are deployed. An engineer creates a new Ingress resource for host network exposure but omits the per-Ingress port annotation. What is the consequence?

options.text: The Ingress falls back to the shared listener port 8080, which is shared across all Ingress resources.
The Ingress is rejected because the host-listener-port annotation is mandatory in this situation.
The Ingress is accepted, but the port clashes are resolved automatically by Cilium.
The Ingress uses the tlsPassthroughPort value as its host listener port.

explanation: The ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation is mandatory when the global mode is dedicated, or when the Ingress sets the loadbalancer-mode annotation to dedicated and multiple Ingress resources are deployed. The port must be unique per Ingress resource, so it cannot simply be shared.

optionRationale.a: Although the default port is 8080, the excerpt states it can only be used for a single Ingress resource as it needs to be unique per Ingress resource, so it cannot be shared across all of them.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt warns that misconfiguration might result in port clashes and instructs the operator to configure unique ports; it does not describe automatic resolution.
optionRationale.d: tlsPassthroughPort is a Helm value for the shared TLS passthrough listener, not a fallback for a dedicated Ingress host listener port.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: This annotation is mandatory if the global Cilium ingress controller mode is configured to ``dedicated`` (``ingressController.loadbalancerMode``) or the ingress resource sets the ``ingress.cilium.io/loadbalancer-mode`` annotation to ``dedicated`` and multiple ``Ingress`` resources are deployed.

stem: You have a local Kubernetes cluster running Cilium and Istio, and you want to follow the demo setup for Istio sidecar mode. Which combination of Helm values must Cilium have been installed with?

options.text: `socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=false`
`socketLB.enabled=false` and `cni.exclusive=true`
`socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=true`
`socketLB.enabled=true` and `cni.exclusive=false`

explanation: The prerequisites state that Cilium must already be installed with the `socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=false` Helm values. Both values must match exactly; changing either one departs from the stated prerequisite.

optionRationale.b: This inverts both values: it disables socket LB and makes the CNI exclusive, neither of which appears in the prerequisites.
optionRationale.c: The socket LB value is right, but ``cni.exclusive`` is set to true rather than the required false.
optionRationale.d: The ``cni.exclusive=false`` part is right, but ``socketLB.enabled=true`` is not the value named in the prerequisites.

citations.title: Prerequisites
citations.quote: Cilium is already installed with the ``socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly`` and ``cni.exclusive=false`` Helm values.

stem: After applying a Cilium-managed L4 network policy restricting the `blue` namespace to clients in `blue` and `red`, the checks behave as expected. You then enhance the policy to a Cilium L7 network policy allowing only the `/ip` URL path. The connectivity checks now show `client 'red' to server 'blue': 503` and `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 503`. What does the excerpt say is the cause, and what must you do to allow Cilium to manage L7 policy?

options.text: The Cilium proxy (HTTP) interferes with Istio's mTLS-based HTTPs connections; you must disable Istio's mTLS authentication by configuring a new policy.
The L4 policy was applied to the wrong namespace; you must reapply it in the `red` namespace.
Istio is in `PERMISSIVE` mode; you must switch it to `STRICT` mode so that mTLS is enforced.
The `/ip` path is not permitted by the Cilium proxy; you must add `/deny` to the allowed paths.

explanation: Once the L7 policy is in place, all communication with the `blue` namespace breaks because the Cilium proxy (HTTP) interferes with Istio's mTLS-based HTTPs connections. The remedy given is to disable Istio's mTLS authentication by configuring a new policy, applied to the same namespace where the HTTP-based network policy is implemented.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not attribute the failure to the policy's namespace placement; it attributes it to the Cilium proxy interfering with Istio's mTLS connections.
optionRationale.c: ``PERMISSIVE`` is the default described earlier and is not presented as the cause of the 503 responses.
optionRationale.d: ``/deny`` is used afterwards to verify that Cilium is enforcing the L7 policy, returning 403; it is not a fix for the 503 responses.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium alongside Istio in ambient mode. They want Cilium L7 HTTP policy to govern traffic for a particular workload, but that workload is currently enrolled in Istio ambient. What must they do so that Cilium can enforce L7 policy on that workload's traffic?

options.text: Remove the workload from Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pods with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`.
Set `mtls.mode=DISABLE` in an Istio PeerAuthentication resource for that workload.
Leave the workload in ambient mode but enable Cilium L7 policy, since Cilium can inspect traffic tunneled over port 15008.
Configure `hostNetwork: true` on the istiod pods so that Cilium can reach the workload's sidecar.

explanation: In ambient mode, the way to make a workload subject to Cilium L7 policy is to take it out of Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pods with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`. Otherwise Istio encrypts the traffic with mTLS and Cilium cannot access it for L7 policy enforcement. Disabling mTLS via PeerAuthentication is the sidecar-mode remedy, not the ambient one.

optionRationale.b: ``mtls.mode=DISABLE`` under PeerAuthentication is the instruction given for sidecar mode, not for ambient mode.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that traffic tunneled and encrypted by Istio over port 15008 gives Cilium no visibility into source, destination or any L7 information, so leaving the workload in ambient does not work.
optionRationale.d: ``hostNetwork: true`` on istiod is a requirement for sidecar mode with automatic injection and Cilium overlay mode, unrelated to L7 policy enforcement.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote:
Ambient: Remove the workloads you wish to manage with Cilium L7 policy from Istio ambient by removing either the
    ``istio.io/dataplane-mode`` label from the namespace,
    or annotating the pods you wish to manage with Cilium L7 with ``ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled``.

stem: An engineer is told that Cilium NetworkPolicy still applies to traffic entering and leaving Istio-managed pods in ambient mode when Istio mTLS and Istio L7 HTTP policy controls are in use. What does the excerpt say Cilium can see of that traffic?

options.text: Cilium sees the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic but has no visibility into its actual source and destination, nor any L7 information.
Cilium sees the full L7 request details because it decrypts the tunnel on port 15008.
Cilium sees nothing at all, so no Cilium NetworkPolicy applies to those pods.
Cilium sees the L4 traffic and the original source and destination, but not the L7 information.

explanation: The excerpt says Cilium NetworkPolicy still applies to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic entering and leaving the Istio-managed pods, but Cilium will have no visibility into the actual source and destination of that traffic, or any L7 information. Istio should therefore enforce policy for traffic between Istio-managed, mTLS-secured workloads at L4 or above.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe Cilium decrypting the tunnel; it states Cilium has no L7 information for that traffic.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly says Cilium NetworkPolicy will still apply to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium has no visibility into the actual source and destination, not merely the L7 information.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote:
Cilium NetworkPolicy will still apply to the encrypted and tunneled L4 traffic entering and leaving the Istio-managed pods,
  but Cilium will have no visibility into the actual source and destination of that tunneled and encrypted L4 traffic, or any L7 information.

stem: A cluster uses Istio in sidecar mode with automatic sidecar injection and Cilium in overlay mode (VXLAN or GENEVE). What does the excerpt require of the `istiod` pods?

options.text: They must be running with `hostNetwork: true` so that they are reachable by the API server.
They must be annotated with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`.
They must have Istio mTLS disabled via `mtls.mode=DISABLE`.
They must be removed from the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` namespace label.

explanation: The excerpt states that when Istio is used in sidecar mode with automatic sidecar injection together with Cilium overlay mode (VXLAN or GENEVE), `istiod` pods must be running with `hostNetwork: true` in order to be reachable by the API server.

optionRationale.b: The ``ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`` annotation is used in ambient mode to keep workloads out of Istio ambient for Cilium L7 policy, not a requirement for istiod in sidecar mode.
optionRationale.c: ``mtls.mode=DISABLE`` is the PeerAuthentication setting for using Cilium L7 policy in sidecar mode, not a requirement on istiod pods.
optionRationale.d: The ``istio.io/dataplane-mode`` label relates to ambient mode enrolment, not to istiod reachability in sidecar mode.

citations.title: Istio configuration
citations.quote: together with Cilium overlay mode (VXLAN or GENEVE), ``istiod`` pods must be running with ``hostNetwork: true`` in order to be reachable by the API server.

stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service and wants the backend Pod to see the client's original address. She is using Cilium Ingress and is deciding whether she must set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on that Service. What does the excerpt say about this requirement?

options.text: It is not necessary, because Cilium ingress traffic is always sent to the local node and forwarded to Envoy via TPROXY, keeping the source IP visible through `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address`.
It is mandatory, because only `Local` prevents masquerading of the source IP for any Service that exposes Envoy.
It is mandatory, because `Cluster` causes the node to always masquerade the source IP for ingress traffic.
It is not necessary, because Cilium rewrites the source IP into the `healthCheckNodePort` response headers instead.

explanation: The excerpt states that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod, via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields. It explains that all ingress traffic bound for a Service that exposes Envoy always goes to the local node and is always forwarded to Envoy using the Linux Kernel TPROXY function.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite for Cilium ingress config: `Local` is not necessary to keep the source IP visible. The masquerading point applies to the general `Cluster` description, not as a mandate for Envoy-exposing Services.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the node *may* masquerade the source IP under `Cluster`, not that it always does, and it explicitly says `Local` is not necessary for Cilium ingress config.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` as the fields carrying the source IP, not the `healthCheckNodePort` response headers.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
However, for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, **it is not
necessary** to configure ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` to keep the source IP
visible to the backend pod (via the ``X-Forwarded-For`` and ``X-Envoy-External-Address``
fields).

stem: A cluster runs `kube-proxy` and exposes a Service with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`. An operator wants to know how to check, from outside the cluster, whether a given node has local Pods behind that Service. According to the excerpt, what behaviour should she expect?

options.text: A request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` returns 200 on nodes with local Pods running and non-200 on nodes without them.
A request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` returns 200 on every node in the cluster regardless of local Pods.
A request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` returns non-200 on nodes with local Pods and 200 on nodes without them.
No such port is opened; the operator must inspect EndpointSlices to determine local Pod presence.

explanation: The excerpt describes part of the contract for `externalTrafficPolicy` local: the node opens a port (the `healthCheckNodePort`, automatically set by Kubernetes when `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is set), and requests to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` return 200 on nodes that have local Pods running and non-200 on nodes that do not.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says non-200 is returned on nodes without local Pods, so 200 on every node is wrong. The always-passing behaviour is described separately for Services exposing Cilium's Envoy.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the reverse: 200 on nodes with local Pods, non-200 on nodes without.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says the node will open the `healthCheckNodePort`, so claiming no such port exists contradicts it.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
the node will
  open a port (the ``healthCheckNodePort``, automatically set by Kubernetes when
  ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` is set), and requests to
  ``http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz`` will return 200 on nodes that
  have local pods running, and non-200 on nodes that don't.

stem: How does the excerpt contrast the `Local` and `Cluster` settings of `externalTrafficPolicy` for a Loadbalancer or NodePort Service?

options.text: `Local` routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, whereas `Cluster` routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly and the node may masquerade the source IP.
`Local` routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, whereas `Cluster` routes only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP.
`Local` routes only to Pods on the local node but always masquerades the source IP, whereas `Cluster` never masquerades the source IP.
`Local` and `Cluster` differ only in the health check port number that Kubernetes assigns automatically.

explanation: The excerpt gives two relevant settings. `Local`: nodes route traffic only to Pods running on the local node, without masquerading the source IP. `Cluster`: the node routes to all endpoints across the cluster evenly, and the node may masquerade the source IP, which in many cases may mean the backend pod does not see the source IP.

optionRationale.b: This swaps the two definitions; the excerpt assigns even cluster-wide routing to `Cluster` and local-only routing to `Local`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says `Local` routes without masquerading the source IP, and that `Cluster` *may* masquerade it, not that it never does.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the `healthCheckNodePort` as automatically set when `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is set; it does not present port numbering as the difference between the two settings.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
- ``Local``: Nodes will only route traffic to Pods running on the local node, 
  *without masquerading the source IP*.
